134483.etyen:
Borrowed from Dutch waker (“wind indicator; buoy”) or Low German waker (“wind indicator; buoy”). The source noun is derived from the nautical verb waken (“to float; remain above water”), which is etymologically the same word as waken (“to be awake; keep watch”). The verb continues Middle Dutch wāken, from Old Dutch wacon, from Proto-Germanic *wakāną (“to be awake, watch”), ultimately from *weǵ- (“to be lively, awake; be strong”).
The Norwegian verb vake (“to float; remain afloat; rise to the surface”) was likewise borrowed from Dutch or Low German and belongs to the same word family as inherit

63571.etyen:
The lowercase form of U. From Latin V, from an Old Italic form of Ancient Greek Υ (U, “upsilon”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤅 (w, “waw; hook”). In medieval Latin-script writing, ⟨u⟩ and ⟨v⟩ were positional forms of a single letter; they later became distinct letters, with ⟨u⟩ used for the vowel. / The uppercase form of u. From Latin V, as a later rounded graphic variant of the same letter, from an Old Italic form of Ancient Greek Υ (U, “upsilon”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤅 (w, “waw; hook”), from Proto-Canaanite , from Proto-Sinaitic , from Egyptian 𓌉 representing a mace.
In Latin, ⟨V⟩ originally represented both the vowel /u/ and the consonant /w/; the distinct letterforms ⟨U⟩ and ⟨V⟩ became conventional from the 16th century.

1000019.etyen:
Derived from French Tunisie (“Tunisia”), from Tunis and -ie (“country-name-forming suffix”). The city name is ultimately from Arabic تُونِس (tūnis, “Tunis”). Its deeper origin is uncertain; proposed explanations connect the name with a Berber word tns (“encampment”), or with the Phoenician goddess Tanit and the ancient city Tynes.
Compare the parallel adaptations Norwegian Nynorsk Tunisia, Danish Tunesien, Swedish Tunisien, English Tunisia and Italian Tunisia.

Probably from Italian Italia (“Italy”); the exact immediate route into Norwegian is not securely documented. Another ancient explanation associates the name with a people called the Itali. The name originally denoted the southern tip of the Italian peninsula and was gradually extended northwards.
